credit_frameworks.title: The Frameworks for Higher Education Qualifications of UK Degree-Awarding Bodies (second edition, February 2024)
credit_frameworks.issuer: Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education (QAA)

statements.fact: One credit equals 10 notional hours of learning
statements.quote: The various credit frameworks used within the UK operate according to the same underpinning principles (for example, one credit equates to 10 notional hours of learning).

statements.fact: The FHEQ itself is not a credit framework; England uses the QAA credit framework of 2021
statements.quote: The FHEQ is a qualifications framework, based on the outcomes represented by the main qualification titles. It is not an integrated credit and qualifications framework, nor is its use dependent on credit. ... A revised higher education credit framework for England was published by QAA in 2021, and all degree-awarding bodies in England and Northern Ireland that award credit are able to reference this framework as it is designed to be complementary to the FHEQ.

statements.fact: Scotland and Wales use integrated credit frameworks (SCQF, CQFW)
statements.quote: The SCQF and the CQFW are integrated credit and qualifications frameworks which means that they specify minimum credit volumes and levels for qualifications

statements.fact: Bachelor’s with honours: three or four full-time years
statements.quote: Bachelor's degrees with honours form the largest group of higher education qualifications. Typically, learning outcomes for these courses would be expected to be achieved on the basis of study equivalent to three or four full-time academic years and lead to qualifications with titles such as Bachelor of Arts, BA (Hons) or Bachelor of Science, BSc (Hons).
statements.location: Level 6 / SCQF Level 10 qualification descriptor, para c), p. 22 [PDF p. 24]

statements.fact: Minimum credit for a bachelor’s degree with honours by jurisdiction
statements.quote: Bachelor's degrees with honours (eg BA/BSc Hons) | FHEQ level 6 | SCQF level 10 | England/Northern Ireland: 360 (90 at FHEQ Level 6) | Scotland: 480d (90 at SCQF Level 10) | Wales: 360 (90 at FHEQ Level 6 and a max of 30 at CQFW Level 3) | ECTS point ranges from the QF-EHEA: 180-240 ECTS points
statements.location: Annex C table (minimum credit requirements), p. 42 [PDF p. 44]; table cells joined with | by the collector

statements.fact: Scottish honours degrees are one year longer
statements.quote: d These qualifications in Scotland are a year longer than their counterparts in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
statements.location: Notes to Annex C table, note d, p. 43 [PDF p. 45]

statements.fact: Ordinary (non-honours) bachelor’s degree minimum credit
statements.quote: Bachelor's degrees | 9 | 300 (60 at FHEQ Level 6) | 360 (60 at SCQF Level 9) | 300 (60 at FHEQ Level 6 and a max of 30 at CQFW Level 3)

statements.fact: OfS uses a version of the credit table as a sector-recognised standard in England
statements.quote: Annex C of this document sets out the minimum credit requirements specified by the relevant credit frameworks for each of the jurisdictions in the UK. In England, the OfS has adopted a version of this table as a component of its sector-recognised standards.

credit_frameworks.title: Higher Education Credit Framework for England: Advice on Academic Credit Arrangements (2021)

statements.fact: One credit = 10 notional hours
statements.quote: Credit value The number of credits, at a particular level, assigned to a body of learning. The number of credits is based on the estimated learning hours (where one credit typically represents 10 notional hours of learning).

statements.fact: Notional learning hours definition
statements.quote: Notional learning hours The number of hours which it is expected that a learner (at a particular level) will spend, on average, to achieve the specified learning outcomes at that level. This may include time spent in class, directed learning, independent study and assessment. One credit is typically described as being equal to 10 hours of notional learning.

statements.fact: A 20-credit module equals 200 hours
statements.quote: Credit assigned to modules or courses is based on the approximate number of hours a learner is expected to spend learning to achieve the learning outcomes for that module, including guided and independent study. For example, a 20-credit module equates to 200 hrs, divided into different modes of learning.

statements.fact: Bachelor’s with honours: 360 credits, 90 at level 6; first cycle, 180-240 ECTS
statements.quote: Bachelor’s degrees with honours (eg BA/BSc Hons) | FHEQ Level 6 | Minimum credit 360 (90 at FHEQ level 6) | First cycle (end of cycle) qualifications | 180-240 ECTS credits
statements.location: Credit Framework for England 2021 table, p. 8 [PDF p. 10]; table cells joined with | by the collector

statements.fact: Values in the table are minimums
statements.quote: Values shown in column 3 are the minimum that are typically associated with the qualification (plus any permissible minimum or maximum at a specified level shown in parentheses).

statements.fact: 120 credits in a typical academic year
statements.quote: To achieve this, providers need a clear understanding of both the level and the quantity of academic credit being studied, and how this compares to more established models based on the study of 120 credits in a typical academic year.
statements.location: Alignment of credit with flexible learning models, p. 13 [PDF p. 15]

statements.fact: Two UK credits = one ECTS credit; 60 ECTS = one full-time year
statements.quote: ECTS is based on the principle that 60 ECTS credits are equivalent to the learning outcomes and associated workload of a typical full-time academic year of formal learning. In everyday practice, two UK credits are equivalent to one ECTS credit.

statements.fact: A 360-credit honours degree equates to 180 ECTS
statements.quote: For example, a bachelor’s degrees with honours in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, with a typical total volume of at least 360 credits, equate to 180 ECTS credits as long as the learning outcomes are consistent with the relevant Dublin descriptor.

credit_frameworks.title: Making Use of Credit: A Companion to the Higher Education Credit Framework for England (2021)

statements.fact: Accelerated two-year degrees still carry 360 credits
statements.quote: Accelerated degrees are specifically designed to be delivered in a condensed time period, usually over two-years. ... Award of credit will follow the same pattern as more traditional models, with a typical two-year undergraduate degree consisting of 360 credits.

credit_frameworks.title: Scottish Credit and Qualifications Framework (SCQF): interactive framework page and SCQF credit transfer guidance (updated October 2024)

statements.fact: Scottish honours degree: SCQF level 10, at least 480 credit points
statements.quote: The Scottish Bachelors degree with Honours is designed to SCQF Level 10 and is allocated at least 480 SCQF Credit Points of which a minimum of 90 are at SCQF Level 9 and a minimum of 90 are at SCQF Level 10.
statements.location: Interactive framework page, Level 10, Honours Degree entry

statements.fact: One SCQF credit point = 10 notional hours
statements.quote: 1 SCQF credit point represents 10 notional hours of learning for a typical learner.

statements.fact: Ordinary 360, honours 480
statements.quote: University staff advised Megan that to complete an Ordinary Bachelors degree she would have to complete 360 SCQF Credit Points or if she chose to do an Honours degree she would need to achieve 480 SCQF Credit Points.
statements.location: SCQF credit transfer guidance (Oct 2024), p. 3 (case example)

statements.fact: Four-year duration
statements.location: Not stated as a number of years on the SCQF pages read. The four-year length rests on FHEQ 2024 Annex C note d (These qualifications in Scotland are a year longer than their counterparts in England, Wales and Northern Ireland) together with the three or four years of the FHEQ descriptor; 480 credit points over four years gives 120 per year (arithmetic, not a quoted rule). The Scottish program records in uk_programs.json state the duration as read from each course page.

credit_frameworks.summary: QAA: two UK credits equal one ECTS credit; a 360-credit honours degree equals 180 ECTS; 60 ECTS equal one full-time year. Source: hecf_england_2021, pp. 11 to 12 [PDF pp. 13 to 14]. Under the same 10-hour rule, 360 UK credits equal 3,600 notional hours (arithmetic).

content_themes: 2.1 Construction Management (process management, human resource/people management, construction psychology, planning and scheduling of projects, process performance management)

statements.rule: Scope: Level 4 to honours at Level 6
statements.quote: The CIOB accredits programmes from Regulated Qualificaitons Framework (RQF) Level 4 Higher National Diplomas (HND) to Level 7 Postgraduate Programmes. This framework is for programmes from Level 4 up to honours degree programmes at level 6.
statements.location: 1.2, p. 3 [PDF p. 5]; spelling as in source

statements.quote: the learning outcomes contained in the Education Framework are intended to provide guidance to teaching institutions and should not be viewed or used as a prescribed syllabus.
Institutions are required to meet minimum threshold requirements in core modules across all themes.

statements.rule: Flexibility; grey threshold outcomes at levels 4 and 5
statements.quote: The CIOB does not prescribe how the themes are to be incorporated into the programme and there is not a requirement to meet all of the learning outcomes of the framework in order to achieve accreditation, although it is expected that core modules meet all the threshold outcomes at level 4 and 5, which are highlighted in grey. Flexibility is deliberately built into the Framework to allow institutions greater autonomy in curriculum design.

Although the CIOB does not require that all accredited programmes include a year-long placement, it does strongly advocate the inclusion of such an opportunity. The CIOB does expect that all accredited programmes include suitable WBL elements and opportunities and programmes seeking accreditation are therefore required to identify the WBL elements on the award.

Graduates of accredited degree programmes are granted full exemption and may proceed to Chartered Membership through the Professional Development Programme or by demonstrating the competence requirements through their work experience. All candidates for Chartered Membership are required to pass the Professional Review.
For benchmarking purposes, institutions may wish to refer to the UK QAA benchmark statements for Land, Construction, Real Estate and Surveying

hk_reform.topic: Hong Kong ‘334’ / ‘3+3+4’ New Academic Structure: move of publicly funded bachelor’s degrees from three to four years, first four-year intake September 2012

structure.before: 5 years secondary + 2 years sixth form (HKCEE then HKALE) + 3-year undergraduate degree
structure.after: 3 years junior secondary + 3 years senior secondary (HKDSE) + 4-year undergraduate degree (‘3+3+4’)
structure.source_note: ‘3+3+4’ wording quoted from the LegCo statement of 18 May 2005 and LegCo papers; the ‘before’ line is general knowledge and is not quoted from a saved source

timeline.event: Education Commission sets out proposals for a new senior secondary and higher education academic structure (‘3+3+4’)
timeline.quote: the Education Commission in 2000 set out the blueprint for education development that will meet the challenge of the new century, and in May 2003 set out proposals for developing a new senior secondary and higher education academic structure (‘3+3+4’).
timeline.source: LegCo Panel on Education paper LC Paper No. CB(2) 90/04-05(01), for discussion on 29 October 2004, para. 2

timeline.event: LegCo question LCQ1 ‘Review of academic structure’; reply by the Secretary for Education and Manpower, Professor Arthur K C Li
timeline.quote: The EC confirmed the benefits and practicability of adopting a three-year structure for senior secondary education and a four-year undergraduate programme in Hong Kong.
timeline.source: Education Bureau press archive, LegCo oral reply, 15 October 2003

timeline.event: Consultation document ‘Reforming the Academic Structure for Senior Secondary Education and Higher Education: Actions for Investing in the Future’ launched; three-month consultation to 19 January 2005
timeline.quote: The consultation document proposes a three-year junior secondary and three-year senior secondary education linking to a broader set of post school pathways, including four year undergraduate university programmes, to facilitate improved articulation for students to proceed to further study locally or overseas, to join the workforce or to return to study in future.
timeline.gap: The consultation document itself was not found online; only the LegCo cover paper and the May 2005 Summary of Views (sources/reform/edb_summary_views_master_may05_eng.pdf) were saved.

timeline.event: Decision announced in LegCo and report ‘The New Academic Structure for Senior Secondary Education and Higher Education: Action Plan for Investing in the Future of Hong Kong’ published. New senior secondary to start September 2009; first four-year undergraduate cohort September 2012.
quotes: Taking into account the views of all parties and having balanced various considerations, we have now decided to introduce the new academic structure in September 2009. Current Primary Five students will be the first cohort to benefit from the new senior secondary education. The first cohort of students in the four-years undergraduate programme will begin in September 2012.
For university education, the four-year undergraduate programme will allow more balanced and comprehensive development of our university students.

The new academic structure provides opportunities for all students to receive six-year secondary education and promises to infuse our students with a broadened knowledge base, balanced development, sound language and other generic skills and a propensity for life-long learning.
During the consultation period, we received about 3,300 written submissions

funding.non_recurrent_total_hkd: 7.9 billion (3.5 billion capital for schools and universities; 4.4 billion other non-recurrent)
funding.recurrent_on_full_implementation_hkd: about 2 billion, of which about 1.1 billion for the four-year undergraduate programmes
funding.quote: About $1.1 billion of the recurrent cost is to meet with the additional funding requirements for implementing the four-year undergraduate programmes.

timeline.speaker: Professor Arthur Li, Secretary for Education and Manpower, statement in the Legislative Council
timeline.source: news.gov.hk, ‘On the record’, 18 May 2005; news.gov.hk ‘At school’ item of the same date

timeline.event: Government yearbook records the consensus and the 2012 start
timeline.quote: After years of discussion, there is a general consensus that a three-year curriculum at senior secondary level and a four-year university course will best serve the interests of students in Hong Kong. ... The first four-year undergraduate programme at universities will start in September 2012.
timeline.source: Hong Kong 2005 (HKSAR Government yearbook), Chapter 7 Education

timeline.event: The eight UGC-funded universities announce basic admission criteria for the four-year structure from 2012-13; the Heads of Universities Committee states support for a broad-based curriculum
quotes: The eight universities have announced the basic admission criteria for the four-year undergraduate academic structure to be implemented in the 2012-13 academic year.
It has previously made clear its support of a more broad-based curriculum with more choices for students to suit their individual aptitudes and interests.
timeline.source: news.gov.hk, 5 July 2006, ‘Universities’ basic admission criteria released’

timeline.event: UGC funds institutions to build learning outcomes into the new four-year curriculum
timeline.quote: To facilitate the institutions in weaving ‘outcomes’ into their new four-year curriculum and to build up their capabilities, the UGC is providing additional funding of about $108 million to its funded institutions over the 2006/07 to 2010/11 academic years.
timeline.source: University Grants Committee, Aspirations for the Higher Education System in Hong Kong, December 2010 (LegCo copy CB(2)602/10-11(01)), PDF page 86

timeline.event: First four-year intake and the double cohort: universities admitted the last three-year cohort (HKALE) and the first four-year cohort (HKDSE) in the same year
quotes: from 2012 we will provide a four-year undergraduate programme for students completing the new six-year secondary education curriculum. (In 2012-13 we will concurrently offer a three-year programme, for the last time, to those completing the existing seven-year secondary education curriculum. This is known as the ‘double cohort’.)
By 2012, student numbers at the University will increase by 40–50%, including an extra 3,000 students.

The double cohort year sees the admission of some 2,440 and 2,340 students respectively for the three-year and four-year Bachelor’s degree programmes funded by the University Grants Committee (UGC), while another 1,810 full-time students have been enrolled for UGC-funded higher diploma programmes.

sources.note: first two quotes; the HKU text uses a dash inside the parenthesis, rendered here with a comma

sources.what: PolyU Excel@PolyU, September 2012, ‘PolyU welcomes freshmen of double cohort year’

timeline.gap: No system-wide UGC count of double-cohort first-year places was found; the figures above are for HKU and PolyU only.

timeline.event: Education Bureau concludes the New Academic Structure Medium-term Review (senior secondary side; no change to the four-year degree)

purpose_of_extra_year.summary: Government statements of 2005 give the purpose in general terms (more balanced and comprehensive development, a broadened knowledge base, articulation with other systems). University statements name a broader knowledge base. No saved government or UGC document states in one sentence that the extra year was ‘for general education’; that wording comes from the scholarly literature listed below and was not verified against the article texts.

quotes.quote: For university education, the four-year undergraduate programme will allow more balanced and comprehensive development of our university students.
quotes.source: Secretary for Education and Manpower, LegCo statement, 18 May 2005

quotes.quote: Having an additional undergraduate year will provide students with a more flexible learning experience, giving them time and space to build a broader knowledge base and to develop a more solid foundation for their holistic development.
the new academic structure will provide smoother articulation for further studies or work in Hong Kong and be better connected with other major education systems in the world.
quotes.source: Secretary for Education and Manpower, LegCo statement, 18 May 2005

credit_expectations.general: No system-wide credit rule was found in the saved government sources. Each university set its own four-year framework. The saved programme documents show the current expectations: HKU 240 credits (6-credit courses), PolyU 120 academic credits with a 27-credit General University Requirement, CityU 121 credit units with 31 GE credit units.
